title: Leadership & Life Skills Journey
description: Navigate through life's toughest challenges and build your leadership skills! Every playthrough offers different scenarios — face communication crises, ethical dilemmas, team conflicts, and more. The AI adapts to your choices, creating a unique journey each time while teaching the same core leadership concepts.

storybook_pages.title: Your Leadership Journey Begins
storybook_pages.text: You've just been promoted to lead a growing team. The road ahead is full of challenges — team conflicts, ethical dilemmas, budget crunches, and moments that will define who you are as a leader. Every choice matters.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: a young professional standing at a crossroads with multiple colorful paths ahead, leadership symbols like a compass and lightbulb, motivational cartoon style, vibrant colors

storybook_pages.title: Every Journey Is Different
storybook_pages.text: No two playthroughs are the same. You'll face different challenges each time, but the core lessons remain. Build your influence, keep your team happy, manage your budget, and grow your reputation. Balance is everything.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: a dynamic game board with branching paths, diverse team members around a table, dice and strategy elements, colorful cartoon style, energetic

storybook_pages.title: Rise to the Challenge
storybook_pages.text: Will you lead with empathy or authority? Innovate boldly or play it safe? Prioritize your team or chase results? There's no single right answer — but every choice reveals something about your leadership style.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: a leader standing on a mountain peak with a flag, surrounded by symbols of achievement like trophies and stars, team members cheering below, inspiring cartoon style

how_to_play: Roll the dice and move around the 32-tile board. Each lap earns you +5 Influence and +3 Team Morale.
Land on event tiles to face leadership challenges. Each event has 3-4 choices with very different outcomes.
Only about half the events trigger each playthrough, so every game feels different!
Manage six resources: Influence, Team Morale, Budget, Reputation, Innovation Score, and Work-Life Balance.
Watch out for World Events — economic downturns, team departures, and industry disruptions can shake things up.
Visit the Leadership Workshop to invest in skill-building upgrades.
Face the Board Review challenge to prove your strategic thinking under pressure.
Compete against 3 AI leaders with different styles — can you outperform them all?
Win by reaching the finish tile, having the highest combined score, or unlocking the most achievements.

start.message: A new lap begins! Your team rallies around you. +5 Influence, +3 Team Morale.

rest.message: You take time to recharge. Your team appreciates the break. Balance restored!

treasure.message: Breakthrough moment! Your team's innovation catches the CEO's attention. Budget boost and reputation soar!

tax.message: Company-wide budget cuts hit your department. You lose $8K from your operating budget.

shop_items.description: Invest in a team communication workshop to improve collaboration.

shop_items.label: Innovation Sprint
shop_items.description: Run a week-long innovation sprint to generate breakthrough ideas.

shop_items.label: Team Wellness Program
shop_items.description: Launch a wellness initiative to boost team health and morale.

challenge.question: The board asks: 'Your team's productivity dropped 20% this quarter while morale surveys show 85% satisfaction. What's your diagnosis?'
options: Happy teams aren't always productive — we need clearer goals and accountability
The metrics are wrong — redefine what productivity means for our team
It's a temporary dip from recent changes — give it another quarter
We need to sacrifice some satisfaction for performance targets
challenge.success_message: Excellent analysis! The board is impressed by your ability to balance empathy with accountability.
challenge.fail_message: The board expected deeper analysis. Leadership means seeing beyond surface-level metrics.

power_ups.label: Executive Sprint
power_ups.description: Roll twice and move the total — cover more ground this turn!

power_ups.label: Crisis Shield
power_ups.description: Block the next negative event. Your preparation pays off!

power_ups.label: Strategic Foresight
power_ups.description: See the next 3 tiles ahead so you can plan your moves.

ai_competitors.name: Director Kane
ai_competitors.description: Rules with authority. Prioritizes results over relationships. High risk, high reward leadership.

ai_competitors.name: Manager Priya
ai_competitors.description: Leads with balance. Weighs every decision carefully. Slow and steady wins the race.

ai_competitors.name: Coach Rivera
ai_competitors.description: People-first leader. Invests heavily in team morale and culture, sometimes at the cost of speed.

evt_first_impression.title: First Day as Leader — Making Your Mark
evt_first_impression.story: As the new leader of the student council, you step into the brightly lit room filled with eager faces. Everyone is curious about your vision and how you'll steer the group through the year. The pressure to make a strong first impression weighs heavily on you as you prepare to present your ideas.

choices.text: Present your bold ideas with enthusiasm.
choices.feedback: Your enthusiasm boosts the team's morale, but some members may feel overwhelmed by your ideas.

choices.text: Engage the team in a discussion about their ideas.
choices.feedback: Your willingness to listen fosters a sense of belonging, increasing team morale significantly.

concept_card.definition: The ability to fully focus on, understand, and respond to what is being said.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader who listens to their team's concerns creates a more inclusive environment.

original_event.title: First Day as Leader — Making Your Mark

evt_team_conflict.title: Team Conflict — The Rivalry
evt_team_conflict.story: As the team begins working on the upcoming event, a rivalry flares between two members over differing creative visions. Tensions rise, and you can feel the strain on your team's collaboration. How will you address this conflict to keep the team united?

choices.text: Hold a team meeting to openly discuss the conflict.
choices.feedback: Encouraging open dialogue helps reduce tension, but it requires careful management.

choices.text: Encourage both members to work separately on their ideas and present them.
choices.feedback: This approach fosters creativity but risks deepening the rivalry if not managed well.

concept_card.definition: The process of resolving a dispute or disagreement.
concept_card.real_world_example: Effective leaders mediate conflicts and encourage collaborative solutions.

evt_budget_decision.title: Budget Allocation — Where Does the Money Go?
evt_budget_decision.story: With financial constraints looming, you must allocate the budget wisely for the upcoming projects. Each team member has different priorities, and they’re all vying for your support. How will you navigate this challenging decision?

choices.text: Prioritize funding for the most popular project to keep team morale high.
choices.feedback: While team morale spikes, you may sacrifice the long-term benefits of other crucial projects.

choices.text: Conduct a survey to assess project importance before making decisions.
choices.feedback: Gathering input ensures a more democratic decision but may slow down the process.

concept_card.definition: The ability to plan for the future while anticipating potential challenges.
concept_card.real_world_example: Strategically allocating resources can lead to better outcomes in projects.

original_event.title: Budget Allocation — Where Does the Money Go?

evt_ethical_dilemma_1.title: Ethical Dilemma — The Shortcut
evt_ethical_dilemma_1.story: As deadlines approach, you discover a shortcut that could save time and resources, but it's unethical and could jeopardize the integrity of your team. Faced with this dilemma, you must choose between expedience and ethical leadership.

choices.text: Take the shortcut to meet the deadline, justifying it as a means to an end.
choices.feedback: While you meet the deadline, your reputation takes a hit, and the team may struggle with trust.

choices.text: Refuse the shortcut and communicate the importance of ethical standards to your team.
choices.feedback: Standing up for ethics strengthens your reputation but may pressure your team with tight deadlines.

concept_card.definition: Leading by example and adhering to moral principles in all decisions.
concept_card.real_world_example: An ethical leader prioritizes integrity over convenience, fostering trust within the team.

evt_crisis_management_1.title: Crisis — System Down!
evt_crisis_management_1.story: Just days before the big event, the online system that manages registrations crashes, leaving your team scrambling to find a solution. Time is running out, and your leadership is put to the test. How will you respond to this crisis?

choices.text: Quickly mobilize the team to brainstorm alternative registration methods.
choices.feedback: Your quick action boosts morale and adaptability, but the pressure may lead to exhaustion.

choices.text: Reach out for help from another team or advisor to resolve the issue.
choices.feedback: Utilizing external resources helps in crisis management but may reveal dependency issues.

concept_card.definition: The ability to guide a team effectively during challenging and urgent situations.
concept_card.real_world_example: Crisis leaders maintain clear communication and rally their team to adapt and overcome obstacles.

evt_negotiation_1.title: Negotiation — The Partnership Deal
evt_negotiation_1.story: As your council gears up for the big event, a potential partnership with a local business arises. Their support could provide significant funding, but they have their own demands that might clash with your council's values. You must negotiate terms that benefit both parties while staying true to your mission.

choices.text: Push for a deal that aligns with your values, even if it means less funding.
choices.feedback: Your commitment to your values strengthens the council's reputation but limits financial resources.

choices.text: Accept the business's terms for more funding, despite potential conflicts.
choices.feedback: You secure funding but at the cost of the council's ethical standing.

choices.text: Find a middle ground that satisfies both the business and the council.
choices.feedback: Successfully negotiating a compromise builds your influence and secures needed resources.

concept_card.definition: The process of discussing and reaching an agreement between parties with differing interests.
concept_card.real_world_example: Business negotiations often involve finding a win-win solution that satisfies both parties.

evt_public_speaking_1.title: Public Speaking — The Conference Keynote
evt_public_speaking_1.story: With the event on the horizon, you have been chosen to deliver a keynote address at a local conference. This is a chance to make your council's mission known, but nerves are creeping in as you prepare to speak in front of a large audience.

choices.text: Focus on delivering a polished performance, prioritizing clarity and professionalism.
choices.feedback: A well-delivered speech boosts morale but may come off as too formal.

choices.text: Share personal stories to connect emotionally with the audience.
choices.feedback: Your heartfelt approach resonates well with the audience but leaves you drained afterward.

choices.text: Involve the audience with interactive elements and questions.
choices.feedback: Engaging the audience boosts team morale and fosters a sense of community.

concept_card.definition: The act of performing a speech to a live audience with the goal of informing or persuading.
concept_card.real_world_example: Public speakers often use storytelling to connect with their audience and convey their message.

evt_mentoring_1.title: Mentoring — The Struggling Junior
evt_mentoring_1.story: A junior member of your council is struggling to keep up with the demands of their role. You recognize the potential in them, but they need guidance and support to thrive. This is your chance to embody servant leadership.

choices.text: Offer one-on-one mentoring sessions to help them develop key skills.
choices.feedback: Your investment in their growth strengthens team morale but may stretch your own time thin.

choices.text: Assign them to a more experienced member for guidance.
choices.feedback: Delegating mentorship builds your reputation as a leader who nurtures talent, but may feel like a cop-out.

choices.text: Encourage them to attend workshops and training sessions.
choices.feedback: Encouraging growth through workshops fosters adaptability but might risk their confidence.

concept_card.definition: A relationship in which a more experienced individual provides guidance to a less experienced individual.
concept_card.real_world_example: Mentors often help mentees navigate their careers and develop skills.

evt_innovation_stability_1.title: Innovation vs Stability — The Big Bet
evt_innovation_stability_1.story: As your event approaches, a critical decision arises: should you innovate with a bold new format or stick with the tried-and-true methods that guarantee stability? Weighing the risks involved is essential.

choices.text: Invest in a new format that could attract more attendees but carries risks.
choices.feedback: Taking a risk on innovation could bring excitement but may unsettle your team.

choices.text: Stick with the traditional format that ensures a safe outcome.
choices.feedback: Choosing stability boosts your reputation but may lead to missed opportunities for growth.

choices.text: Conduct a survey to gauge interest in both options before deciding.
choices.feedback: By involving the team in the decision, you enhance morale and ensure a more informed choice.

concept_card.definition: The balance between introducing new ideas and maintaining established practices.
concept_card.real_world_example: Companies often face this dilemma when launching new products vs. relying on proven ones.

original_event.title: Innovation vs Stability — The Big Bet

evt_work_life_1.title: Work-Life Balance — The Weekend Email
evt_work_life_1.story: As you prepare for the upcoming event, an urgent email arrives on the weekend demanding immediate attention. You feel the pressure to respond, but doing so could encroach on your personal time, affecting your work-life balance.

choices.text: Respond immediately to demonstrate your commitment.
choices.feedback: Your promptness is noted, but sacrificing your weekend may lead to burnout later.

choices.text: Wait until Monday to respond, prioritizing your personal time.
choices.feedback: Protecting your downtime helps your well-being but may be seen as unresponsive by some.

choices.text: Draft a brief response indicating you'll address it on Monday.
choices.feedback: Setting expectations with a response fosters understanding and maintains morale.

concept_card.definition: The ability to manage personal and professional responsibilities effectively.
concept_card.real_world_example: Maintaining work-life balance is crucial for overall well-being and productivity.

evt_communication_challenge_1.title: Communication — The Difficult Feedback
evt_communication_challenge_1.story: As you prepare for the big event, you receive feedback about your recent presentation. While some praise your ideas, others express concern about your delivery and engagement. You must communicate this mixed feedback to your team in a way that promotes growth and understanding.

choices.text: Deliver the feedback directly and honestly, emphasizing areas for improvement.
choices.feedback: Your honesty fosters trust, but some team members may feel vulnerable.

choices.text: Focus primarily on the positive aspects to maintain morale.
choices.feedback: While the team feels uplifted, critical growth opportunities may be overlooked.

choices.text: Encourage team members to share their thoughts on the feedback collectively.
choices.feedback: Facilitating a discussion empowers the team, leading to greater collaboration.

concept_card.definition: The ability to recognize and manage your own emotions and the emotions of others.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader who can empathize with their team during stressful times.

evt_team_growth.title: Team Growth — Scaling Up
evt_team_growth.story: As your event draws near, your team has outgrown its initial structure. You must decide how to expand responsibilities and delegate tasks effectively to maintain efficiency and morale.

choices.text: Assign roles based on individual strengths, empowering each member.
choices.feedback: Team members feel valued and engaged, enhancing their performance.

choices.text: Implement a strict hierarchy to ensure tasks are completed faster.
choices.feedback: While tasks are completed quickly, the team feels stifled and disengaged.

choices.text: Encourage team collaboration and shared responsibilities across projects.
choices.feedback: This approach fosters creativity and strengthens team bonds, but may slow progress.

concept_card.definition: A leadership philosophy that prioritizes serving others and meeting their needs.
concept_card.real_world_example: A manager who supports their team's personal and professional development.

evt_ethical_dilemma_2.title: Ethical Dilemma — The Whistleblower
evt_ethical_dilemma_2.story: During a routine check, you discover that a team member has been cutting corners on critical tasks, endangering the integrity of the event. You must decide whether to confront the individual directly, report it to higher authorities, or handle it internally.

choices.text: Confront the team member privately, encouraging them to rectify their actions.
choices.feedback: This approach promotes a culture of transparency, but risks potential conflict.

choices.text: Report the issue to higher authorities without confronting the individual.
choices.feedback: While this action ensures accountability, it may damage relationships and trust.

choices.text: Try to resolve the issue internally by discussing it with the team as a whole.
choices.feedback: This fosters team engagement but may allow the problematic behavior to persist.

concept_card.definition: Leading in a way that is consistent with ethical principles and values.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader who prioritizes honesty and integrity over short-term gains.

evt_negotiation_2.title: Negotiation — Salary Standoff
evt_negotiation_2.story: As you finalize plans for the event, a key member of your team requests a salary increase, citing their increased responsibilities. The negotiation is tense, and you have to balance the budget while maintaining good relations.

choices.text: Offer a modest raise, explaining the budget constraints clearly.
choices.feedback: This maintains transparency and respect, but may not satisfy the team member's expectations.

choices.text: Refuse the request outright due to budget limitations.
choices.feedback: While preserving the budget, you risk damaging morale and losing a valuable team member.

choices.text: Propose a performance-based bonus instead of a salary increase.
choices.feedback: This solution keeps the budget stable while motivating the team member to excel.

concept_card.definition: The process of reaching an agreement through discussion and compromise.
concept_card.real_world_example: A manager negotiating salary terms with an employee.

evt_crisis_management_2.title: Crisis Alert — PR Disaster
evt_crisis_management_2.story: Just days before the event, a damaging article about your organization makes headlines. You must act quickly to manage the public relations disaster and protect your team's reputation.

choices.text: Hold an emergency meeting to address the issue transparently with your team.
choices.feedback: This approach fosters trust and unity, but the crisis is still looming.

choices.text: Draft a public statement denying the claims without addressing the team.
choices.feedback: This may temporarily shield your organization, but it alienates your team.

choices.text: Collaborate with the PR team to create a comprehensive strategy and include your team in the process.
choices.feedback: Involving your team promotes a sense of ownership and resilience against the crisis.

concept_card.definition: The ability to lead effectively during a time of crisis.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader who communicates clearly and decisively during an organizational crisis.

evt_public_speaking_2.title: Public Speaking — The Town Hall
evt_public_speaking_2.story: The day of the event arrives, and you are tasked with speaking at a town hall meeting to address attendees and stakeholders. This is your moment to shine, but nerves and the pressure of expectations weigh heavily on you.

choices.text: Prepare thoroughly and practice your speech multiple times.
choices.feedback: Your thorough preparation shines through, earning respect and boosting your reputation.

choices.text: Speak off-the-cuff to seem relatable.
choices.feedback: While relatable, your lack of preparation leads to a disjointed message, slightly harming your reputation.

choices.text: Invite team members to share their perspectives.
choices.feedback: Including your team highlights collaboration and boosts morale, enhancing your reputation.

concept_card.definition: The act of performing a speech to a live audience.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader engages the audience with a compelling story during a presentation.

evt_mentoring_2.title: Mentoring — The High-Potential Star
evt_mentoring_2.story: As you navigate the complexities of your event planning, a junior team member has shown remarkable potential. Recognizing this, you decide to allocate some time for mentorship. However, balancing this with your responsibilities could strain your already stretched resources.

choices.text: Dedicate time for one-on-one mentoring.
choices.feedback: Your team member feels valued, boosting morale, but your budget constraints tighten.

choices.text: Focus solely on event preparation.
choices.feedback: Neglecting mentorship causes frustration and disengagement in your team.

choices.text: Incorporate mentoring into team meetings.
choices.feedback: Integrating mentoring enhances team cohesion while keeping you on track for the event.

concept_card.definition: A leadership philosophy in which the main goal of the leader is to serve.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader prioritizes their team's needs to empower them to achieve collective goals.

evt_work_life_2.title: Work-Life Choice — The Burnout Signal
evt_work_life_2.story: As the event date looms, you start feeling the weight of stress and exhaustion. Recognizing the signs of burnout in yourself and your team, you must decide how to manage workloads to maintain performance without compromising well-being.

choices.text: Encourage your team to take breaks and recharge.
choices.feedback: Promoting breaks revitalizes your team, enhancing their productivity and morale.

choices.text: Push through the workload to meet deadlines.
choices.feedback: Overworking leads to burnout, decreasing overall morale and productivity.

choices.text: Implement a flexible work schedule.
choices.feedback: A flexible approach allows your team to manage their time effectively, boosting morale.

concept_card.definition: The equilibrium between personal life and career work.
concept_card.real_world_example: An employee practices time management to ensure they have quality family time after work.

evt_innovation_stability_2.title: Innovation Lab — The Disruptive Idea
evt_innovation_stability_2.story: During a brainstorming session, a team member proposes a radical idea that could either revolutionize your event or create chaos. You must decide how to approach this disruptive suggestion while maintaining stability.

choices.text: Encourage exploration of the idea with a pilot project.
choices.feedback: Pilot projects foster innovation and team excitement, balancing risk with potential reward.

choices.text: Reject the idea outright to maintain current plans.
choices.feedback: Dismissing the idea stifles creativity and lowers team morale.

choices.text: Request modifications to make it more feasible.
choices.feedback: Modifying the idea encourages innovation while ensuring alignment with current plans.

concept_card.definition: The process of guiding individuals and teams through organizational change.
concept_card.real_world_example: A manager implements changes gradually to help the team adapt smoothly to new procedures.

evt_communication_challenge_2.title: Communication — The Cross-Team Misunderstanding
evt_communication_challenge_2.story: Just as your team gears up for the event, a miscommunication arises between two departments regarding their roles. This misunderstanding could jeopardize the event's success and your leadership reputation.

choices.text: Facilitate a cross-department meeting to clarify roles.
choices.feedback: Clarifying roles boosts team morale and strengthens your reputation as a leader.

choices.text: Send an email with clarifications.
choices.feedback: While it resolves some issues, it lacks the personal touch needed to ensure full understanding.

choices.text: Ignore the misunderstanding and hope it resolves itself.
choices.feedback: Ignoring the issue leads to greater confusion and damages your reputation.

concept_card.definition: A belief that one will not be penalized or humiliated for speaking up.
concept_card.real_world_example: A team member feels safe to share ideas during a meeting, knowing their opinion is valued.

evt_team_conflict_2.title: Team Conflict — The Remote vs Office War
evt_team_conflict_2.story: As the event approaches, a rift emerges between team members who prefer remote work and those advocating for in-office collaboration. Tensions rise, impacting team morale and focus. You must step in to mediate and restore harmony before it escalates further.

choices.text: Facilitate a team discussion to openly address the concerns of both sides.
choices.feedback: Your proactive approach fosters understanding and improves relationships.

choices.text: Implement a hybrid working model that accommodates both preferences.
choices.feedback: By finding a compromise, you create a more flexible work environment.

choices.text: Encourage team members to communicate their struggles one-on-one.
choices.feedback: Personalized attention helps address issues but may take time away from project tasks.

concept_card.definition: The process of resolving a dispute or disagreement.
concept_card.real_world_example: A manager mediates a disagreement between two employees to restore a collaborative atmosphere.

original_event.title: Team Conflict — The Remote vs Office War

evt_budget_decision_2.title: Budget Dilemma — Investment Trade-off
evt_budget_decision_2.story: Facing a budget shortfall, you must decide whether to cut costs on marketing or reduce the event's scale. Each option has significant implications for the team's morale and the event's impact.

choices.text: Invest in marketing to ensure a larger turnout, risking the event's quality.
choices.feedback: While risking quality, you could gain visibility and attract more participants.

choices.text: Scale back the event to maintain quality and control costs.
choices.feedback: Quality remains high, but it may disappoint team members expecting a bigger event.

choices.text: Conduct a team vote to gauge preferences on budget allocation.
choices.feedback: Involving the team fosters trust, but it may slow down the decision-making process.

concept_card.definition: The process of maintaining healthy relationships with those affected by a project.
concept_card.real_world_example: A project manager regularly updates stakeholders about budget decisions and changes to maintain trust.

evt_crisis_management_3.title: Crisis — Key Team Member Poached
evt_crisis_management_3.story: In a shocking turn of events, a key team member has accepted a lucrative offer from a competitor just weeks before the event. You now face the challenge of keeping the team motivated while finding a replacement.

choices.text: Hold a team meeting to openly discuss the situation and brainstorm solutions together.
choices.feedback: Transparency builds trust and encourages teamwork in resolving the crisis.

choices.text: Reach out to your network for potential candidates to fill the role quickly.
choices.feedback: Leveraging your connections could yield fast results, but it may strain existing relationships.

choices.text: Delegate more responsibilities to other team members to compensate for the loss.
choices.feedback: By trusting your team more, you empower them, though it may lead to burnout.

concept_card.definition: The ability to lead effectively during turbulent times.
concept_card.real_world_example: A leader manages team dynamics and maintains focus during a sudden crisis.

evt_difficult_stakeholder.title: Stakeholder Management — The Unreasonable Request
evt_difficult_stakeholder.story: A key stakeholder presents an unreasonable request that could jeopardize the integrity of the event. You must navigate this delicate situation to uphold ethical standards while maintaining the relationship.

choices.text: Politely decline the request and propose an alternative that aligns with your values.
choices.feedback: Standing firm on your principles strengthens your reputation amongst the team and stakeholders.

choices.text: Negotiate with the stakeholder to find a middle ground that satisfies both parties.
choices.feedback: Effective negotiation can maintain a positive relationship while achieving a fair compromise.

choices.text: Gather feedback from the team on how to handle the request before responding.
choices.feedback: Involving the team can lead to a more informed decision and improve morale.

concept_card.definition: The process of managing the expectations and influence of stakeholders in a project.
concept_card.real_world_example: A project manager balances stakeholder demands with ethical considerations to ensure project integrity.

evt_diversity_inclusion.title: Diversity & Inclusion — The Hiring Decision
evt_diversity_inclusion.story: You're hiring for a critical role. Candidate A has perfect technical skills but would make your team even more homogeneous. Candidate B brings diverse perspective and strong (not perfect) skills.

choices.label: Hire Candidate A — skills are what matter most right now
choices.feedback: Short-term skills gained, long-term innovation and perspective lost. Homogeneous teams hit ceilings.

choices.label: Hire Candidate B — diverse teams outperform in the long run
choices.feedback: Candidate B brings fresh viewpoints that challenge groupthink. Three months in, they're your most creative contributor.

choices.label: Negotiate budget to hire both
choices.feedback: Expensive but your team gets both skills AND diversity. Investment in people always compounds.

choices.label: Hire A now, create an internship pipeline for diverse talent
choices.feedback: Pragmatic approach. You solve today's need while building tomorrow's pipeline. Long-term thinking.

evt_failure_recovery.title: Failure Recovery — The Failed Project
evt_failure_recovery.story: A project your team spent 4 months on has been cancelled by leadership. Morale is crushed. People feel their work was wasted. How do you help the team recover?

choices.label: Run a thorough retrospective — extract every lesson learned
choices.feedback: The retro reveals 10 actionable insights. The project failed but the lessons will prevent future failures.

choices.label: Celebrate the effort — throw a team event to honor the hard work
choices.feedback: Your team is surprised and moved. Celebrating effort, not just outcomes, builds a resilient culture.

choices.label: Immediately pivot to a new exciting project — no time to mourn
choices.feedback: The new project is exciting but unprocessed grief lingers. People need closure before new beginnings.

choices.label: Be transparent about why it was cancelled and advocate for the team's recognition
choices.feedback: Leadership acknowledges the team's excellent work despite the cancellation. Your advocacy matters.

evt_delegation.title: Delegation — Letting Go of Control
evt_delegation.story: You're stretched thin. Three critical projects need leadership. You can't effectively lead all three. But delegating means trusting others with your reputation.

choices.label: Keep all three — you can handle it, just need more hours
choices.feedback: You're everywhere and nowhere at once. Quality drops across all three. Overcommitment isn't leadership.

choices.label: Delegate two projects to capable team members
choices.feedback: Your delegates rise to the occasion. You focus on what only you can do. Multiplication through trust.

choices.label: Delegate one, co-lead one, solo-lead the most critical
choices.feedback: Balanced approach. You prioritize while developing others. Practical leadership wisdom.

evt_feedback_culture.title: Building Feedback Culture — The Tough Conversation
evt_feedback_culture.story: Your team avoids giving each other feedback. Everyone is polite but problems fester. You want to build a culture of radical candor but it feels risky.

choices.label: Model it first — publicly ask for feedback on YOUR leadership
choices.feedback: Your vulnerability is contagious. When the leader asks for feedback first, everyone feels safe to follow.

choices.label: Bring in a coach to train the team on feedback frameworks
choices.feedback: Structured frameworks help. People learn to separate behavior from identity. Skills are buildable.

choices.label: Start with anonymous feedback tools — build safety first
choices.feedback: Anonymous feedback surfaces truth but can enable sniping. A stepping stone, not the destination.

choices.label: Mandate feedback in every meeting — make it a habit
choices.feedback: Forced feedback feels performative. People say nice things to check the box. Culture can't be mandated.

evt_change_management.title: Change Management — The Big Restructure
evt_change_management.story: Upper management is restructuring. Your team will merge with another department. New processes, new reporting lines, new culture clash. Your team is anxious.

choices.label: Embrace it enthusiastically — change is opportunity
choices.feedback: Your positivity helps but feels forced to anxious team members. Change management requires empathy first.

choices.label: Build bridges — organize joint social events with the other team
choices.feedback: Social bonds form before formal structures. When the merge happens, it feels like joining friends. Brilliant.

choices.label: Advocate for your team's interests in the new structure
choices.feedback: Your team feels protected. Key roles and projects are preserved. Political skill is leadership skill.

choices.label: Push back on the restructure — argue it's unnecessary
choices.feedback: You fight the tide and lose. Upper management notes your resistance. Sometimes you must adapt, not resist.

evt_trust_building.title: Trust Building — The Vulnerability Moment
evt_trust_building.story: In a team meeting, a member shares they're struggling with a personal issue affecting their work. The room goes quiet. Everyone looks at you. This moment will define your team's culture.

choices.label: Share your own vulnerability — normalize being human at work
choices.feedback: Your openness transforms the team culture. People bring their whole selves to work. Psychological safety achieved.

choices.label: Thank them for sharing and offer concrete support resources
choices.feedback: Professional and compassionate. Resources help without overstepping boundaries. Solid leadership.

choices.label: Move on politely and follow up with them privately later
choices.feedback: The private follow-up helps them, but the team saw you deflect a vulnerable moment. Opportunity missed.

evt_competing_priorities.title: Competing Priorities — The Triple Bind
evt_competing_priorities.story: You have three urgent requests from three different VPs, all due this week. Your team can only fully deliver one. The others need to be delayed or simplified.

choices.label: Prioritize based on business impact — be transparent about trade-offs
choices.feedback: Your data-driven prioritization earns respect. Two VPs are disappointed but understand. Leadership is choosing.

choices.label: Try to deliver all three — your team can handle it
choices.feedback: All three delivered, all three mediocre. Your team is exhausted and resentful. Overcommitting helps no one.

choices.label: Negotiate with the VPs to stagger deadlines
choices.feedback: Masterful stakeholder management. Staggered deadlines mean quality delivery for all. Everyone wins.

evt_recognition.title: Recognition — Who Gets the Credit?
evt_recognition.story: Your team just delivered a huge win. The CEO wants to know who was responsible. You could take the credit (you did lead it), give credit to the team, or highlight the quiet contributors.

choices.label: Accept the credit — you led this, you deserve recognition
choices.feedback: Your star rises but your team feels invisible. They'll remember who took the bow.

choices.label: Give all credit to the team — leadership is about them
choices.feedback: Your team is recognized and motivated to deliver again. And the CEO sees a leader who builds others up.

choices.label: Highlight the quiet contributors who usually go unnoticed
choices.feedback: The unsung heroes are finally seen. This single act changes how they show up every day. Profound leadership.

choices.label: Share credit equally — this was a true team effort
choices.feedback: Fair and diplomatic. Everyone gets mentioned. A bit generic, but no one feels left out.

evt_difficult_decision.title: Difficult Decision — Letting Someone Go
evt_difficult_decision.story: Despite months of coaching, a team member isn't meeting expectations. They're a good person but wrong for the role. Keeping them hurts the team. Letting them go hurts them.

choices.label: Have the difficult conversation — help them find a better fit elsewhere
choices.feedback: The hardest conversation you've had. But you handle it with dignity. They thank you a year later.

choices.label: Keep them — you can't bring yourself to let someone go
choices.feedback: Compassionate but unfair to them and the team. Sometimes kindness means making hard calls.

choices.label: Find them an internal transfer to a better-suited role
choices.feedback: They thrive in the new role. What looked like failure was just misalignment. Empathetic and strategic.

evt_vision_setting.title: Vision Setting — Charting the Course
evt_vision_setting.story: The team needs a new 12-month vision. You could set it yourself (faster), co-create it with the team (slower but more buy-in), or bring in an external facilitator.

choices.label: Set the vision yourself — leaders lead
choices.feedback: Clear and decisive. But your team feels like passengers, not drivers. Compliance without commitment.

choices.label: Facilitate a team workshop to co-create the vision
choices.feedback: Two days of intense work produces a vision everyone owns. Commitment beats compliance every time.

choices.label: Bring in an external facilitator for fresh perspective
choices.feedback: The facilitator challenges assumptions you didn't know you had. Expensive but transformative.

world_events.title: Economic Downturn — Budgets Frozen!
world_events.description: A market downturn hits the industry. All departments face budget freezes and hiring stops. Do more with less.

world_events.title: Key Team Member Quits!
world_events.description: A valued team member accepts an offer elsewhere. Workload redistributes across the remaining team.

world_events.title: Viral Success — You're Trending!
world_events.description: Your team's work goes viral on social media. Recognition pours in from across the industry.

world_events.title: Industry Disruption — New Technology Emerges!
world_events.description: A breakthrough technology threatens to make current approaches obsolete. Adapt or fall behind.

world_events.title: Merger Opportunity — Teams Combining!
world_events.description: Corporate announces a potential merger. Uncertainty is high but opportunities for growth exist.

world_events.title: New Regulations — Compliance Required!
world_events.description: New government regulations require process changes and compliance training across all teams.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to recognize, understand, and manage your own emotions while also recognizing and influencing the emotions of others.
glossary_terms.example: A leader notices a team member is unusually quiet in a meeting and checks in with them privately afterward.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: EQ is your emotional radar — it helps you read the room and respond with empathy.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Daniel Goleman's research (1995) showed EQ accounts for 67% of abilities needed for leadership effectiveness—more than technical skill or IQ. The four domains are: self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, and relationship management.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Satya Nadella credits his 'learn-it-all' over 'know-it-all' philosophy—rooted in EQ—for Microsoft's cultural transformation from a stagnant to a $3T company.

glossary_terms.definition: A leadership philosophy where the leader's primary goal is to serve their team, removing obstacles and empowering others to do their best work.
glossary_terms.example: Instead of taking credit for a win, a servant leader highlights their team's contributions to the CEO.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Servant leaders flip the pyramid — they work FOR their team, not the other way around.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Robert Greenleaf coined 'servant leadership' in 1970: leaders serve their teams rather than the other way round. A servant leader prioritises growth and wellbeing of team members. Research by Ken Blanchard Associates found servant-led teams have 50% higher engagement and 30% lower turnover than traditional command-and-control teams.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Herb Kelleher built Southwest Airlines on servant leadership — treating employees better than customers, on the premise that happy employees create happy customers. Southwest was consistently profitable for 47 consecutive years (1973–2019) while competitors went bankrupt multiple times.

glossary_terms.definition: A team environment where people feel safe to take risks, ask questions, admit mistakes, and share ideas without fear of punishment or humiliation.
glossary_terms.example: In a psychologically safe team, someone can say 'I made a mistake' without worrying about being fired or mocked.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: If people are afraid to speak up, you only hear what they think you want to hear.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Google's Project Aristotle (2016) found psychological safety—the belief you won't be punished for speaking up—was the #1 predictor of high-performing teams, above individual talent or IQ.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Amy Edmondson found that hospital units with higher error-reporting rates had better patient outcomes—because psychologically safe teams caught mistakes before they compounded.

glossary_terms.definition: A feedback framework that combines caring personally about someone with challenging them directly. It's being honest because you care, not despite caring.
glossary_terms.example: Telling a colleague 'Your presentation structure was confusing — here's how I'd restructure it' rather than just saying 'Great job!'
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Radical Candor = caring enough to be honest. Ruinous Empathy = being too nice to be helpful.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Kim Scott's framework balances two axes: caring personally about people AND challenging them directly. Most managers fail by either ruinous empathy (caring but not challenging — giving vague feedback to avoid discomfort) or obnoxious aggression (challenging but not caring — being brutally honest without regard for feelings). Only direct + caring feedback produces growth.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: At Apple, Scott observed Steve Jobs use radical candor directly — he challenged teams brutally but was deeply invested in their success. In contrast, she watched a Google manager tell an employee their PowerPoint presentations were 'brilliant' when they were terrible, delaying the employee's growth for months.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through dedication, hard work, and learning. Opposite of a fixed mindset that sees talent as innate.
glossary_terms.example: Instead of 'I'm not a public speaker,' a growth mindset says 'I'm not a good public speaker YET.'
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Add 'yet' to any limitation. 'I can't do this... yet.' That's growth mindset.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Carol Dweck's 35 years of research show that believing abilities can be developed (growth mindset) leads to higher achievement, more resilience, and better collaboration than believing intelligence is fixed.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: After years of struggling, Jordan adopted a 'process over results' mindset and turned 6 NBA finals failures into fuel—not evidence of fixed limits.

glossary_terms.definition: The act of entrusting tasks or responsibilities to team members while maintaining accountability. Effective delegation develops people and multiplies output.
glossary_terms.example: Instead of reviewing every document yourself, you trust a senior team member to handle reviews and only escalate concerns.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Delegation isn't dumping work — it's investing trust and developing your team's capabilities.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Delegation is not abdication. The Delegation Matrix distinguishes four levels: tell (decide and instruct), sell (decide and persuade), consult (gather input before deciding), and delegate (hand over full decision). Leaders must match the level to each person's competence and commitment. Under-delegation creates bottlenecks; over-delegation creates chaos.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Andy Grove at Intel documented how managers must delegate routine decisions while retaining strategic ones. He coined 'OKRs' (Objectives and Key Results) as a delegation tool — giving teams direction while measuring outcomes rather than controlling process. John Doerr brought OKRs to Google in 1999; they are now used by thousands of companies.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of identifying, analyzing, and strategically engaging people who have influence over or are affected by your team's work.
glossary_terms.example: Before launching a new process, you identify which executives need to approve it, which teams are affected, and how to communicate with each.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Every project has visible and invisible stakeholders. Miss one and your project could derail.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: R. Edward Freeman's Stakeholder Theory (1984) argues organisations must create value for all stakeholders — employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and shareholders — not just shareholders. Leaders who ignore non-shareholder stakeholders create short-term gains at the cost of long-term value destruction. The Business Roundtable endorsed this view in 2019.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol recall in 1982 is the gold standard. When seven people died after cyanide-laced capsules appeared in Chicago stores, J&J recalled all 31 million bottles nationally ($100M loss) before knowing the full scope. CEO James Burke prioritised customers over shareholders. J&J's share price recovered within months; trust was preserved for decades.

glossary_terms.definition: The capacity to recover quickly from setbacks, adapt to change, and keep going in the face of adversity. A core leadership skill during times of uncertainty.
glossary_terms.example: After a major project cancellation, a resilient leader processes the disappointment, extracts lessons, and energizes the team for the next challenge.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Resilience isn't about never falling — it's about how quickly you get back up.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Resilience in leadership has three components: absorb (maintaining function under pressure), adapt (changing behaviour when old approaches stop working), and transform (using adversity as a catalyst for growth). The American Psychological Association distinguishes resilience from mental toughness — resilience involves asking for help and processing emotion, not suppressing it.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Howard Schultz returned to lead Starbucks in 2008 during the financial crisis when the company had opened too many stores too fast. Rather than simply cutting costs, he closed stores for a day to retrain all baristas, eliminated unhealthy menu items, and refocused on coffee craft — a transformation that grew share price 10× by 2019.

glossary_terms.definition: A communication technique where you fully concentrate on what someone is saying, understand their message, respond thoughtfully, and remember the conversation.
glossary_terms.example: Instead of thinking about your response while someone talks, you focus entirely on their words, ask clarifying questions, and paraphrase to confirm understanding.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Active listening means listening to understand, not listening to respond.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Active listening means listening to understand rather than to respond. Research by Zenger/Folkman found that leaders in the top 5% of listening had teams with 40% higher engagement scores. Active listening involves reflecting back what you heard ('What I'm hearing is...'), asking follow-up questions, and resisting the urge to problem-solve prematurely.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Indra Nooyi, former PepsiCo CEO, wrote personal letters to the parents of her senior executives thanking them for raising good people. She credited this habit of deeply listening to people's lives — beyond their professional roles — as central to her leadership style. PepsiCo's revenues grew 80% during her tenure.

glossary_terms.definition: A leadership approach where you adapt your style based on the maturity and skill level of your team members. New members need direction; experienced ones need autonomy.
glossary_terms.example: You give detailed instructions to a new hire but only set goals for a veteran — each gets what they need to succeed.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: There's no one-size-fits-all leadership style. Read the person, adapt the approach.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Hersey and Blanchard's Situational Leadership model says no single leadership style works for all situations. The appropriate style depends on the follower's competence (skill) and commitment (motivation) for a specific task. Low skill + high motivation requires directing; high skill + low motivation requires coaching; high skill + high motivation requires delegating.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: New surgeons are directed closely through every step of an operation (high task structure). Senior surgeons are delegated full autonomy (low supervision). A senior surgeon learning a new technique reverts to needing more guidance. Effective chiefs of surgery switch styles fluidly, matching the situational leadership model precisely.

win_conditions.description: Navigate the board, face leadership challenges, and reach the Summit tile. Win by reaching the finish, achieving the highest combined score across all resources, or unlocking the most achievements. Every choice shapes your leadership legacy!

emotional_intelligence.definition: The ability to recognize, understand, and manage your own emotions, and to recognize, understand and influence the emotions of others.
emotional_intelligence.example: When you notice a team member is frustrated and address it with empathy before it escalates.
emotional_intelligence.deep_dive: Daniel Goleman's research found EI accounts for 67% of the abilities required for superior leadership performance — twice as important as technical expertise. EI has four components: self-awareness (knowing your emotions), self-management (controlling them), social awareness (reading others), and relationship management (influencing others). Unlike IQ, EI can be significantly improved with practice.
emotional_intelligence.real_world_example: Satya Nadella transformed Microsoft from a stagnant giant to a $3 trillion company by leading with empathy, shifting the culture from 'know-it-all' to 'learn-it-all'. He credits reading books on empathy — including one about raising his son with disabilities — as the turning point in his leadership.

active_listening.definition: Fully concentrating on what is being said rather than passively hearing. Involves reflecting, paraphrasing, and asking clarifying questions.
active_listening.example: Scheduling 1-on-1s and truly listening to concerns before jumping to solutions.
active_listening.deep_dive: Studies show people remember only 25-50% of what they hear. Active listening closes that gap through specific techniques: maintain eye contact, avoid interrupting, ask open-ended follow-up questions, and paraphrase what you heard. The hardest part? Suppressing the urge to formulate your response while the other person is still talking.
active_listening.real_world_example: Oprah Winfrey's legendary interview skills — built on radical active listening — helped her become the first Black female billionaire. Bill Gates holds 'Think Weeks' in isolation specifically to listen to ideas without distraction. Great listeners don't just hear words; they read the space between them.

servant_leadership.definition: A leadership philosophy where the main goal is to serve others. Servant leaders share power, put employees' needs first, and help people develop and perform.
servant_leadership.example: A manager who removes obstacles for their team rather than just assigning tasks.
servant_leadership.deep_dive: Robert Greenleaf coined the term in 1970, arguing the best leaders ask 'How can I serve?' rather than 'How can I lead?' Research consistently shows servant-led organizations outperform command-and-control structures on employee satisfaction, retention, and customer loyalty. The paradox: leaders gain MORE power when they give it away.
servant_leadership.real_world_example: Howard Schultz built Starbucks into a global brand by pioneering healthcare and stock options for part-time employees — radical in retail. Alan Mulally at Ford refused executive bonuses during the 2008 crisis, choosing to be paid like his workers. Both leaders saw employee satisfaction drive customer satisfaction drive profit.

psychological_safety.definition: A shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — speaking up, asking questions, or admitting mistakes without fear of punishment.
psychological_safety.example: Creating team norms where 'bad news' is welcomed and people feel safe to disagree.
psychological_safety.deep_dive: Harvard professor Amy Edmondson coined this term after a counterintuitive finding: the best-performing hospital teams reported MORE errors than poor teams. Not because they made more mistakes — but because they felt safe admitting them. Google's two-year Project Aristotle study confirmed this across 180 teams: psychological safety was the single biggest predictor of team effectiveness.
psychological_safety.real_world_example: NASA's Challenger disaster in 1986 was partly caused by engineers who felt unable to voice safety concerns to management. The same pattern appeared at Boeing with the 737 MAX. In contrast, Pixar's 'Braintrust' meetings — where anyone can critique any project without hierarchy — have produced hit after hit because ideas are judged on merit, not who said them.

stakeholder_management.definition: The process of identifying, analyzing, planning, and engaging with individuals who can influence or be affected by your decisions.
stakeholder_management.example: Mapping out who needs to be informed, consulted, or given decision-making power for a project.
stakeholder_management.deep_dive: The RACI framework (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) is the gold standard for stakeholder clarity. But mapping isn't enough — stakeholders need different engagement styles: high-power/high-interest stakeholders need active management; low-power/low-interest just need monitoring. Failing to manage stakeholders is the #1 reason projects fail, according to PMI research.
stakeholder_management.real_world_example: Jeff Bezos's 'working backwards' approach at Amazon starts with a press release written from the customer's perspective before a single line of code is written. Elon Musk's turbulent stakeholder management at Twitter (X) showed what happens when key stakeholders — advertisers, employees, regulators — are alienated simultaneously. Managing relationships isn't optional; it's the job.

conflict_resolution.definition: The methods and processes used to facilitate the peaceful ending of conflict and retribution. Key approaches include mediation, negotiation, and collaborative problem-solving.
conflict_resolution.example: When two team members disagree, facilitating a structured conversation where both sides feel heard.
conflict_resolution.deep_dive: The Thomas-Kilmann model identifies five conflict styles: Competing, Collaborating, Compromising, Accommodating, and Avoiding. Most people default to one style, but expert leaders switch based on context. Research shows unresolved workplace conflict costs US businesses $359 billion annually in lost productivity. The key insight: most conflict is about unmet needs, not differing opinions.
conflict_resolution.real_world_example: Nelson Mandela used negotiation and reconciliation to transition South Africa from apartheid without the predicted civil war — considered impossible at the time. At Apple, Steve Jobs and Jony Ive famously clashed repeatedly, but Jobs created a structure where productive creative tension led to legendary products rather than destructive conflict.

situational_leadership.definition: Adapting your leadership style based on the competence and commitment of the person you're leading. Different situations require different approaches.
situational_leadership.example: Giving detailed guidance to a new hire while allowing an experienced team member autonomy.
situational_leadership.deep_dive: Hersey and Blanchard's model defines four styles: Directing (high task, low relationship), Coaching (high task, high relationship), Supporting (low task, high relationship), and Delegating (low task, low relationship). The key variable is the follower's 'development level' — their skill AND will for the specific task. Great leaders diagnose before they prescribe.
situational_leadership.real_world_example: Phil Jackson won 11 NBA championships by adapting his coaching style to each player — structured triangle offense for the team, but different communication styles with Michael Jordan's competitiveness vs. Shaq's need for affirmation. Fauci's approach during COVID changed as the crisis evolved — directive in early stages, collaborative later as science developed.

delegation.definition: Assigning responsibility and authority to others to complete tasks. Effective delegation develops people, builds trust, and multiplies your impact.
delegation.example: Entrusting a team lead to run a project meeting instead of doing it yourself.
delegation.deep_dive: The #1 failure mode of new managers is the inability to delegate — doing work they should hand off, becoming a bottleneck. Effective delegation means assigning outcomes, not tasks, with clear authority and accountability. The paradox: delegating makes you more powerful as a leader, not less. A team of 10 that's fully empowered multiplies your throughput 10x.
delegation.real_world_example: Richard Branson has built 400+ companies while traveling and kite-surfing — through radical delegation. He says: 'Find people who are better than you at specific things, and get out of their way.' Warren Buffett delegates all operational decisions at Berkshire's 60+ subsidiaries, focusing only on capital allocation — the highest-leverage activity.

growth_mindset.definition: The belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through dedication, hard work, and learning from failure. Opposite of a 'fixed mindset.'
growth_mindset.example: Treating a project failure as a learning opportunity rather than a career-ending mistake.
growth_mindset.deep_dive: Carol Dweck's 30 years of Stanford research found that fixed mindset people avoid challenges (to protect their identity as 'smart'), while growth mindset people seek challenges as how they get smarter. The neurological basis: growth mindset learners show greater brain activity when processing mistakes. The good news: mindset is malleable — even believing you can change your mindset is a growth mindset act.
growth_mindset.real_world_example: Satya Nadella replaced Ballmer's 'know-it-all' culture with 'learn-it-all' — Microsoft's market cap went from $300B to $3T. Michael Jordan was cut from his high school basketball team. Edison made 1,000 unsuccessful attempts before the lightbulb. Dweck's research on Chicago high school students showed those with growth mindsets recovered from a 'not yet' grade to pass algebra at far higher rates than fixed mindset peers.

ethical_leadership.definition: Leading by example through morally appropriate conduct — honesty, fairness, respect for others, and principled decision-making even when it's costly.
ethical_leadership.example: Turning down a lucrative shortcut because it violates company values or harms stakeholders.
ethical_leadership.deep_dive: Ethics isn't just about avoiding harm — it's a competitive advantage. Research shows ethical companies attract better talent, maintain customer trust longer, and recover from crises faster. The Edelman Trust Barometer consistently shows trust is the most valued corporate asset. Ethical lapses, conversely, compound: they attract regulatory scrutiny, talent attrition, and customer exodus simultaneously.
ethical_leadership.real_world_example: Paul Polman (Unilever) refused quarterly earnings guidance and focused on decade-long sustainability — the stock tripled. Johnson & Johnson's 1982 Tylenol recall (pulling $100M product without government mandate) is now a Harvard Business School ethics case: the short-term hit rebuilt lasting trust. Enron's executives earned billions through fraud — and watched the company evaporate in months.

change_management.definition: A structured approach to transitioning individuals, teams, and organizations from a current state to a desired future state. Key to navigating transformation.
change_management.example: When restructuring, communicating the 'why' clearly, providing support, and celebrating early wins.
change_management.deep_dive: Kotter's 8-Step Change Model is the most validated framework: Create urgency → Build a coalition → Form a vision → Communicate it → Remove obstacles → Create quick wins → Build on the wins → Anchor change. The #1 failure mode is skipping step 1 — people don't change without feeling the urgency is real. McKinsey research finds 70% of change programs fail, primarily due to employee resistance and lack of management support.
change_management.real_world_example: When Apple transitioned from PowerPC to Intel chips, Steve Jobs managed developer anxiety with precise communication, emulators, and a year of runway. When Lou Gerstner took over IBM in 1993 (losing $8B annually), he spent his first 100 days listening before announcing change — then rebuilt methodically. Ford's Alan Mulally used weekly 'Business Plan Reviews' to create radical transparency that reversed a $17B loss.

feedback_culture.definition: An environment where giving and receiving constructive feedback is normalized, valued, and happens regularly — not just during annual reviews.
feedback_culture.example: Implementing regular retrospectives where everyone shares what went well and what to improve.
feedback_culture.deep_dive: Kim Scott's 'Radical Candor' framework defines the ideal as 'caring personally while challenging directly.' The failure modes: Ruinous Empathy (caring but too afraid to challenge), Obnoxious Aggression (challenging without caring), or Manipulative Insincerity (neither). Research shows frequent feedback increases performance 12% more than annual reviews, yet 65% of employees say they want more feedback than they receive.
feedback_culture.real_world_example: Netflix's 'keeper test' — 'Would I fight to keep this person?' — and their norm of 360-degree feedback at all levels has produced a culture credited for their extraordinary innovation pace. Bridge Partners found that leaders who actively seek feedback have teams that are 20% more engaged. Ray Dalio's Bridgewater operates on radical transparency — every meeting is recorded and feedback is expected to be direct and data-driven.

strategic_thinking.definition: The ability to think long-term, see the big picture, anticipate trends, and make decisions that align short-term actions with long-term goals.
strategic_thinking.example: Choosing to invest in technical debt reduction now to move faster in 6 months.
strategic_thinking.deep_dive: Strategic thinking differs from strategic planning: planning is about executing a known strategy; thinking is about questioning whether the strategy is right. The three time horizons (McKinsey): H1 (optimize today), H2 (build tomorrow), H3 (create future options). Great strategic thinkers constantly toggle between these. The risk: organizations naturally focus on H1 and under-invest in H3 until a competitor disrupts them.
strategic_thinking.real_world_example: Amazon operated at a loss for years — Bezos prioritized H3 (AWS, logistics network, Prime flywheel) over H1 profits. This patience created a $2T company. Kodak invented the digital camera in 1975 but buried it to protect film margins — the ultimate failure of strategic thinking. Nokia dominated mobile phones but couldn't see the smartphone H3, ceding to Apple.

work_life_balance.definition: The equilibrium between time spent on work and personal life. For leaders, it also means modeling healthy boundaries for your team.
work_life_balance.example: Not sending work emails after 7 PM and encouraging your team to fully disconnect on weekends.
work_life_balance.deep_dive: The research is unambiguous: sustained overwork reduces productivity. Microsoft Japan's 4-day work week experiment increased productivity by 40%. Stanford research shows output drops sharply after 55 hours per week, and productivity after 70 hours is no more than 55. Leaders who model balance create permission for their teams to recharge — which is when insight, creativity, and resilience are rebuilt.
work_life_balance.real_world_example: Arianna Huffington collapsed from exhaustion and broke her cheekbone in 2007, then founded Thrive Global to combat burnout. Jeff Bezos famously protects his 8 hours of sleep, calling it his most important 'productivity tool.' Denmark consistently tops happiness and productivity rankings, with an average 33-hour workweek proving that sustainable output beats maximum hours.

crisis_leadership.definition: The ability to lead effectively during emergencies — making rapid decisions under pressure, communicating clearly, and maintaining team confidence.
crisis_leadership.example: When systems go down, staying calm, delegating clearly, and communicating transparently with stakeholders.
crisis_leadership.deep_dive: Crisis leadership has three phases: Response (contain the crisis), Recovery (restore stability), and Renewal (build back stronger). The biggest mistake leaders make: communicating too late or too little. Research on airline disasters found the critical variable wasn't the crisis itself but whether crew communicated clearly under pressure. The same holds for business: the coverup is always worse than the crime.
crisis_leadership.real_world_example: Jacinda Ardern's response to the 2019 Christchurch shooting — swift, empathetic, decisive — became a global case study in crisis leadership. She appeared in public immediately, changed gun laws within days, and never once used the attacker's name. Johnson & Johnson's Tylenol crisis vs. Enron's Enron: one company chose transparency and survived; the other chose concealment and collapsed.

transformational_leadership.definition: A leadership style that inspires positive changes in followers. Transformational leaders are energetic, enthusiastic, and passionate about the vision.
transformational_leadership.example: Inspiring your team to adopt a new methodology by connecting it to a bigger purpose.
transformational_leadership.deep_dive: Transformational leadership (Bass, 1985) operates on four dimensions — the 4 I's: Idealized Influence (being a role model), Inspirational Motivation (articulating compelling vision), Intellectual Stimulation (challenging assumptions), and Individualized Consideration (coaching each person). Meta-analyses show transformational leaders produce 20-30% higher team performance than transactional (reward/punishment) leaders.
transformational_leadership.real_world_example: Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech is the archetype: a specific, vivid vision that moved millions. Steve Jobs transformed Apple twice — from a failing company in 1997 to the world's most valuable, then from computers to the iPhone era. Satya Nadella's transformation of Microsoft's culture shows that transformational leadership applies equally to 180,000-person organizations as to small teams.

win_criteria.label: Best Resource Balance
win_criteria.description: Lowest variance across all resource growth percentages

transfer_exercises.game_context: Your leadership style adapted to different team crises and scenarios.
transfer_exercises.real_world: This week, consciously try a different communication style with someone you typically struggle to connect with.
transfer_exercises.challenge: Practice the 'balcony view': in your next meeting, spend 5 minutes observing group dynamics before speaking. What patterns do you notice?

transfer_exercises.game_context: You managed team trust during high-pressure moments.
transfer_exercises.real_world: After your next difficult conversation, write down: what you felt, what you wanted to say, and what you actually said. Notice the gap.
transfer_exercises.challenge: This week: identify one relationship that's fraying. Initiate one genuine, non-task-related conversation with that person.

transfer_exercises.game_context: You balanced short-term crisis management with long-term vision.
transfer_exercises.real_world: Map your current responsibilities on a 2×2 urgency/importance matrix. Which quadrant are you spending the most time in?

cultural_context: Adaptive leadership — the ability to lead effectively through change and ambiguity — is among the most sought-after competencies in India's corporate and public sector. India's organisations face constant disruption from technology, policy, and market changes.
reflection_prompt: Which turn was your turning point — and was it skill, luck, or planning?
